newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election campaign hots up as left gains.
newsitem.headline: French election campaign hots up as left gains.

text.p: An opinion poll showing France's left-wing parties catching up with the ruling centre-right majority has injected a new breath of excitement into the country's general election campaign which officially opens on Monday

The poll, published in the Sunday newspaper Le Journal du Dimanche, showed the left would win between 255 and 285 seats and the centre-right between 269 and 299 seats in the 577-member National Assembly.
The same poll conducted a week ago gave the left between 219 and 245 seats and the centre-right between 311 and 331 seats.

"The campaign which so far had seemed unable to find its rhythm or themes has bounced back...with the possibility that the left might get a majority in metropolitan France," Le Journal du Dimanche commented.
The poll, conducted by the IFOP group, did not include the 22 assembly seats for France's remaining overseas possessions.
The newspaper said that if the left-wing trend continued, "the 22 overseas seats will play a decisive role".
This opened the possibility, often mentioned but never put to the test, that France's political fate might depend on votes of South Seas islanders, the last to vote because of different time zones.
The official campaign begins at midnight (2200 GMT) once all candidacies have been registered.

Political leaders have already started to criss-cross the country to hold meetings, but there is wide agreement the campaign has been bland with much blame going to Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Socialist opposition chief Lionel Jospin, leaders of their respective camps.

Opinion polls show the French at large would have preferred former European Commission president Jacques Delors as leader of the left instead of Jospin, who is often seen as a lacklustre intellectual out of touch with everyday public concerns.
The dry Juppe is the most unpopular prime minister in nearly 40 years, with opinion polls showing the public often describing him as arrogant and unlikeable.
Dozens of youths gathered on Friday night outside a restaurant in Bordeaux, where he is mayor, to throw eggs and water at him as he emerged.

But Le Journal du Dimanche noted that even if the left outstripped the right at the polls, the situation would be far from smooth for the new majority, which would have to cohabit uneasily with President Jacques Chirac for the remaining five years of his seven-year term in office.
The left's main force, the Socialists, would also be at the mercy of their uneasy Communist and ecologist allies to stay in power.
The conservative daily Le Figaro said Chirac, always a highly effective campaigner, would intervene in the campaign on Wednesday to shore up his faltering backers.
This was denied by his office but Juppe said he would consider it normal for Chirac to step into the fray.
Asked by the Journal du Dimanche if he wanted Chirac's aid, Juppe replied: "It's up to him to decide.

"But I would like to note that General de Gaulle, Georges Pompidou, Valery Giscard d'Estaing and Francois Mitterrand (Chirac's predecessors as president) all expressed themselves publicly several times during general elections. It is normal the president should say what he thinks and what he would like to see happen," Juppe said.

Five members of extreme-rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front party were lightly hurt when they were attacked by about 20 ultra-leftists while handing out leaflets at an open-air market in the northern city of Lille, police said.
Le Pen is to hold an election rally in Lille on Wednesday.
